title: Two Sum
description: Given an array of integers and a target value, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Assume exactly one valid answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice.
constraints:
2 <= nums.length <= 10^4
-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9
Only one valid answer exists
hints: Brute force checks every pair — that's O(n^2). Can you trade space for time?
A hash map lets you check 'have I seen target - current number before?' in O(1).
Iterate once, storing each number's index in a map as you go, and check the complement before inserting the current number.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
description: Given an array where each element is a stock's price on that day, find the maximum profit from a single buy followed by a single sell. If no profit is possible, return 0.
constraints:
1 <= prices.length <= 10^5
0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4

examples.explanation: Buy on day 2 (price 1), sell on day 5 (price 6), profit = 5
Prices only fall, so no transaction is profitable

hints: Track the lowest price seen so far as you scan left to right.
At each day, the best possible profit if you sold today is price minus the minimum seen so far.
Keep a running maxProfit and update it each day in a single pass — O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Product of Array Except Self
description: Given an array, return a new array where each element is the product of all elements except itself, without using division and in O(n) time.
constraints:
2 <= nums.length <= 10^5
-30 <= nums[i] <= 30
The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer

examples.explanation: Each output[i] is the product of all other elements
Any zero in the array forces most outputs to zero

hints: Without division, think in terms of prefix and suffix products.
Build an array of products of everything to the left of each index, then multiply in products of everything to the right.
You can do the right-side pass with a single running variable instead of a second array, getting O(1) extra space excluding the output.

title: Valid Palindrome
description: Given a string, determine if it's a palindrome after converting all letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters.
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 2*10^5
s consists of printable ASCII characters

examples.input: s = "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
examples.explanation: Cleaned: 'amanaplanacanalpanama', which reads the same forward and backward
Cleaned: 'raceacar', which is not a palindrome

hints: You don't need to build the cleaned string first — you can skip non-alphanumeric characters while comparing.
Use two pointers starting at both ends, moving inward.
Skip invalid characters from either side before comparing, and stop as soon as a mismatch is found.

testCases.input: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

title: Container With Most Water
description: Given an array of heights representing vertical lines, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container holding the maximum amount of water.
constraints:
2 <= height.length <= 10^5
0 <= height[i] <= 10^4

examples.explanation: Lines at index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7) give area = min(8,7) * (8-1) = 49
Only one container possible: min(1,1) * 1 = 1

hints: Brute force checks every pair — O(n^2). Look for a way to eliminate pairs without checking them.
Start with two pointers at the far ends; the width is currently maximal, so only height limits the area.
Move the pointer at the shorter line inward — moving the taller one can never increase the area, since width only shrinks.

title: 3Sum
description: Given an array of integers, find all unique triplets that sum to zero.

examples.explanation: These are the only two unique triplets that sum to 0
No triplet sums to 0

hints: Sort the array first — this makes both duplicate-skipping and two-pointer scanning possible.
Fix one number, then use two pointers on the remaining sorted subarray to find pairs summing to its negation.
After finding a valid triplet, skip over duplicate values for all three pointers to avoid repeated triplets.

title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
description: Given an array of integers and an integer k, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size k.

examples.explanation: Subarray [5,1,3] has the maximum sum of 9
Subarray [3,4] has the maximum sum of 7

hints: Recomputing the sum for every window from scratch is O(n*k) — wasteful.
As the window slides by one position, you only add one new element and remove one old element.
Maintain a running window sum: subtract the element leaving the window, add the one entering it, and track the max.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
description: Given a string, find the length of the longest substring that contains no repeating characters.
constraints:
0 <= s.length <= 5*10^4
s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces

examples.explanation: The longest substring without repeats is 'abc', length 3
The longest substring without repeats is 'b', length 1

hints: Checking every substring is O(n^2) or worse — think about growing and shrinking a window instead.
Keep a set (or a map of last-seen index) of characters currently in the window.
When you see a repeat, shrink the window from the left until the repeat is removed, then keep expanding from the right while tracking the max window length.

title: Minimum Window Substring
description: Given strings s and t, find the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t (including duplicates). Return an empty string if no such window exists.
constraints:
1 <= s.length, t.length <= 10^5
s and t consist of English letters

examples.explanation: 'BANC' is the smallest window containing all of A, B, and C
t needs two a's but s only has one, so no valid window exists

hints: This is a variable-size sliding window problem — track character counts needed vs. counts currently in the window.
Expand the right edge until the window satisfies all of t's character counts, then try shrinking from the left while it still satisfies them.
Every time the window is valid, check if it's the smallest seen so far before continuing to shrink.

title: Contains Duplicate
description: Given an array of integers, determine if any value appears at least twice.

examples.explanation: 1 appears twice
All elements are distinct

hints: Sorting first turns this into an adjacent-comparison problem, but costs O(n log n).
A hash set can check membership in O(1), giving an O(n) solution overall.
Walk through the array once, adding each number to a set — if a number is already in the set, return true immediately.

title: Group Anagrams
description: Given an array of strings, group the anagrams together. Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same frequencies.
constraints:
1 <= strs.length <= 10^4
0 <= strs[i].length <= 100
strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Words with identical sorted-letter forms are grouped together
A single empty string forms its own group

hints: Two strings are anagrams exactly when they have the same 'signature' — think about what that signature could be.
Sorting each string's characters gives a canonical key that's identical for all anagrams of each other.
Use a hash map from that canonical key to a list of original strings, then return the map's values.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers, in O(n) time.

examples.explanation: The longest consecutive run is [1,2,3,4]
The longest consecutive run is [0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]

hints: Sorting works but costs O(n log n) — the problem asks for O(n), so think about a hash set instead.
Put every number in a hash set, then only start counting a sequence from numbers that are the start of a run (i.e. num-1 is not in the set).
From each valid start, keep checking num+1, num+2, ... in the set and track the longest run found.

title: Sort Colors
description: Given an array with only values 0, 1, and 2 (representing red, white, blue), sort it in-place so equal values are adjacent, in a single pass without using a library sort.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 300
nums[i] is 0, 1, or 2

examples.explanation: The array sorted in ascending order of 0, 1, 2
Already only three distinct values, sorted in one pass

hints: A counting sort (count 0s, 1s, 2s, then overwrite) works but takes two passes — can you do it in one?
This is the Dutch National Flag problem — maintain three pointers: low, mid, high.
Swap nums[mid] with nums[low] or nums[high] depending on its value, moving low/mid forward or high backward, until mid passes high.

title: Merge Sorted Array
description: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2, merge nums2 into nums1 in-place so that nums1 becomes one sorted array. nums1 has enough trailing space to hold all elements.
constraints:
nums1.length == m + n
nums2.length == n
0 <= m, n <= 200

examples.explanation: The merge of [1,2,3] and [2,5,6]
Nothing to merge in

hints: Merging from the front requires shifting elements — expensive. Try merging from the back instead.
Since nums1 has empty trailing space, you can place the largest remaining element (from either array) at the very end each step.
Use three pointers: one at the end of the real nums1 elements, one at the end of nums2, and one at the very end of the array, moving all leftward.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
description: Given an unsorted array and an integer k, find the kth largest element (not the kth distinct element) without necessarily sorting the whole array.

examples.explanation: Sorted descending: [6,5,4,3,2,1], the 2nd largest is 5
Sorted descending: [6,5,5,4,3,3,2,2,1], the 4th largest is 4

hints: Full sort works in O(n log n), but you don't actually need the whole array sorted.
A min-heap of size k tracks the k largest elements seen so far — the top of the heap is the answer.
Alternatively, Quickselect (a variant of quicksort's partition step) finds the kth largest in average O(n) time.

title: Reverse Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]
-5000 <= Node.val <= 5000

examples.explanation: Each node's next pointer is reversed
An empty list reversed is still empty

hints: Think about what you need to remember before you overwrite a node's next pointer.
Keep three pointers: previous, current, and next, and rewire one link at a time.
Iterate until current becomes null, then previous is your new head.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
constraints:
The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50]
-100 <= Node.val <= 100
Both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: Merging both sorted lists in order
Both empty, result is empty

hints: A dummy head node avoids special-casing which list starts first.
Walk both lists simultaneously, always attaching the smaller current node next.
Once one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other list directly — it's already sorted.

title: Linked List Cycle
description: Given the head of a linked list, determine if the list has a cycle in it, without using extra memory proportional to the list length.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4]
-10^5 <= Node.val <= 10^5

examples.input: head = [3,2,0,-4], with a cycle back to index 1
examples.explanation: The tail connects back into the list, forming a cycle
Single node with no cycle

hints: Using a hash set to track visited nodes works but uses O(n) space — can you do it in O(1)?
Floyd's cycle detection: use two pointers, one moving one step at a time, one moving two steps at a time.
If there's a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer and they'll meet.

title: Valid Parentheses
description: Given a string containing just the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string has valid, properly nested and matched brackets.
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 10^4
s consists only of bracket characters

examples.explanation: Every open bracket is closed by the same type in the correct order
Mismatched bracket types

hints: A stack naturally models 'most recently opened bracket must close first'.
Push opening brackets; when you see a closing bracket, check if it matches the top of the stack.
If the stack is empty when you need to pop, or non-empty at the end, the string is invalid.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression given in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix), where operands and operators are provided as an array of tokens.
constraints:
1 <= tokens.length <= 10^4
Each token is an operator (+, -, *, /) or an integer

examples.explanation: 4 + (13 / 5) = 4 + 2 = 6 (integer division)

hints: Postfix notation is built exactly for stack-based evaluation.
Push numbers onto the stack; when you hit an operator, pop the top two, apply the operator, and push the result back.
Watch division order — the second-popped operand is the left-hand side of the operation.

title: Implement Queue using Stacks
description: Implement a first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue using only two stacks, supporting push, pop, peek, and empty operations.
constraints:
1 <= number of calls <= 100
All operations are valid (pop/peek only called on non-empty queue)

examples.explanation: peek() returns 1 (front), pop() removes and returns 1, empty() is false since 2 remains
pop() removes and returns the only element

hints: One stack alone reverses order — you need a way to 'undo' that reversal.
Use an 'in' stack for pushes and an 'out' stack for pops/peeks.
When 'out' is empty and you need to pop or peek, dump all of 'in' into 'out' — this reverses the order back to FIFO.

title: Implement Stack using Queues
description: Implement a last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack using only queues, supporting push, pop, top, and empty operations.
constraints:
1 <= number of calls <= 100
All operations are valid

examples.explanation: top() and pop() both return the most recently pushed element, 2
pop() removes and returns the only element

hints: A single queue can simulate a stack if you rotate it after every push.
After pushing a new element, rotate the queue by (size - 1) so the new element moves to the front.
This makes the most recently pushed element always the front of the queue, giving LIFO order with pop/top in O(1).

title: Sliding Window Maximum
description: Given an array and a window size k, return an array of the maximum value in each sliding window as it moves from left to right across the array.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
1 <= k <= nums.length

examples.explanation: The max of each window of size 3 as it slides across
Single-element window

hints: A brute-force max per window is O(n*k) — think about what info you can reuse between windows.
Use a deque storing indices, keeping it in decreasing order of value from front to back.
Before adding a new index, pop smaller values off the back (they can never be the max again); pop the front if it's fallen outside the window.

title: Design Circular Queue
description: Design a fixed-size circular queue supporting enqueue, dequeue, front, rear, isEmpty, and isFull operations, all in O(1) time.
constraints:
1 <= queue capacity <= 1000
0 <= value <= 1000
At most 3000 operation calls

examples.input: CircularQueue(3), enqueue(1), enqueue(2), enqueue(3), enqueue(4), rear()
examples.explanation: enqueue(4) fails because the queue (capacity 3) is full; rear() still returns 3
After dequeuing, there's room again

hints: A fixed-size array with head and count (or head and tail) pointers avoids shifting elements.
Use modular arithmetic to wrap indices around: (index + 1) % capacity.
Track the count of elements (or a head/tail plus a full flag) to distinguish an empty queue from a full one, since both can have head == tail.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth — the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [0, 10^4]
-100 <= Node.val <= 100

examples.explanation: The longest path is 3 -> 20 -> 15 (or 7), which has 3 nodes
An empty tree has depth 0

hints: Think recursively: the depth of a tree is 1 plus the deeper of its two subtrees.
depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(node.left), depth(node.right)), with depth(null) = 0 as the base case.
This can also be done iteratively with a level-by-level (BFS) traversal, counting levels.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree, where every node's value is strictly between the min and max bounds implied by its ancestors.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4]
-2^31 <= Node.val <= 2^31 - 1

examples.explanation: 1 < 2 < 3, valid BST ordering
Node 4's left child is 3, and while 3 < 4 locally, node 4 sits in the right subtree of 5 where all values must exceed 5

hints: Just checking node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val locally isn't enough — bounds must propagate from ancestors.
Pass down a valid (min, max) range as you recurse: the left subtree must stay below the current node, the right subtree above it.
An in-order traversal of a valid BST also produces strictly increasing values — that's an alternative check.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
description: Given a BST and two nodes p and q, find their lowest common ancestor — the deepest node that has both p and q as descendants.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10^5]
All node values are unique
p and q both exist in the tree

examples.explanation: 6 is the split point where 2 and 8 diverge into different subtrees
A node can be a descendant of itself

hints: Unlike a general binary tree, a BST's ordering tells you which direction to go without searching both subtrees.
Starting at the root, if both p and q are less than the current node, go left; if both are greater, go right.
The first node where p and q are no longer both on the same side (or one equals the current node) is the LCA.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
description: Design a class that, given an initial array of integers and an integer k, supports adding new numbers one at a time and always returns the current kth largest element after each addition.
constraints:
1 <= k <= 10^4
0 <= initial array length <= 10^4
-10^4 <= values <= 10^4
At least k elements will exist in the stream when add() is first called

examples.input: KthLargest(3, [4,5,8,2]), add(3), add(5), add(10), add(9), add(4)
examples.explanation: After each add, the 3rd largest value among all numbers seen so far
With k=1, the answer is just the running maximum

hints: You don't need to re-sort the entire stream on every add — think about maintaining only what's necessary.
Keep a min-heap of size k containing the k largest elements seen so far; its top (minimum) is the kth largest.
When a new number arrives, push it in; if the heap grows past size k, pop the smallest.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
description: Given an array of integers, return the k most frequent elements, in any order.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^5
k is in the range [1, number of distinct elements]

examples.explanation: 1 appears 3 times, 2 appears 2 times — the two most frequent
Only one distinct element

hints: First count frequencies with a hash map — that part is straightforward.
Rather than fully sorting all distinct values by frequency (O(n log n)), a heap of size k gets you O(n log k).
Bucket sort by frequency (bucket index = count, values 0..n) gives an O(n) alternative, since frequency is bounded by array length.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
description: Given an array of k sorted linked lists, merge them all into one sorted linked list and return its head.

examples.explanation: Merging all three sorted lists into one
No lists to merge

hints: Merging two lists at a time pairwise across all k lists works — think about the best order to do the merges in.
A min-heap holding the current front node of each list lets you always pick the smallest next node in O(log k).
Alternatively, merge lists pairwise in a divide-and-conquer fashion — merging in pairs and repeating gives O(n log k) total, the same complexity as the heap approach.

title: Binary Search
description: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the index of the target if found, otherwise -1. Solve in O(log n) time.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
-10^4 <= nums[i], target <= 10^4
All values in nums are unique and sorted in ascending order

examples.explanation: 9 exists in nums and its index is 4
2 does not exist in nums so return -1

hints: Linear scan is O(n) — the sorted property lets you eliminate half the search space each step.
Maintain low and high pointers; compare the target to the middle element to decide which half to keep.
Be careful with the midpoint calculation and updating low/high to avoid infinite loops or off-by-one errors.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Given a sorted array that has been rotated at an unknown pivot, and a target value, search for the target in O(log n) time.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 5000
-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
All values are unique
nums is a rotated ascending array

examples.explanation: 0 is found at index 4
3 is not present

hints: Even though the whole array isn't sorted, at least one half of any subarray you're looking at is always sorted.
Compare nums[mid] to nums[low] to determine which half is the sorted one.
If the target falls within the sorted half's range, search there; otherwise search the other half.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Given a rotated sorted array with unique elements, find the minimum element in O(log n) time.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 5000
-5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000
All values are unique

examples.explanation: The array was rotated so the minimum, 1, sits mid-array
The minimum is 0

hints: The minimum is the only element smaller than both its neighbors (or the array isn't rotated at all).
Compare nums[mid] to nums[high] — if nums[mid] > nums[high], the minimum is to the right of mid; otherwise it's at or to the left of mid.
Narrow the search range using this comparison until low and high converge.

title: Subsets
description: Given an array of unique integers, return all possible subsets (the power set), without duplicates.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10
All elements are unique

examples.explanation: All 2^3 = 8 possible subsets
A single element has 2 subsets: empty and itself

hints: Each element has exactly two choices: include it in the current subset, or don't.
Backtrack through the array: at each index, recurse once including the element and once excluding it.
Alternatively, build subsets iteratively by doubling the existing list each time you add a new number.

title: Permutations
description: Given an array of unique integers, return all possible permutations, in any order.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 6
All elements are unique

examples.explanation: All 3! = 6 orderings of the array
Both orderings of a 2-element array

hints: Backtracking: build a permutation one position at a time, choosing from the remaining unused numbers.
Track which numbers have already been placed (a 'used' boolean array or a set), and remove/restore them as you recurse and backtrack.
When the current permutation reaches the full length, record a copy of it before backtracking further.

title: Combination Sum
description: Given an array of distinct positive integers and a target, return all unique combinations where the chosen numbers sum to the target. The same number may be reused unlimited times.
constraints:
1 <= candidates.length <= 30
2 <= candidates[i] <= 40
All elements of candidates are distinct
1 <= target <= 40

examples.explanation: 2+2+3=7 and 7=7 are the only combinations summing to 7
Three distinct combinations reach 8, reusing numbers as needed

hints: Since numbers can repeat, at each recursive step you can either move to the next candidate or reuse the current one.
To avoid generating the same combination in different orders (like [2,3] and [3,2]), only allow choosing candidates at or after your current starting index.
Sorting the candidates first lets you stop early (prune) once the running sum exceeds the target.

title: Climbing Stairs
description: You're climbing a staircase with n steps, taking either 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return how many distinct ways you can climb to the top.

examples.explanation: Two ways: (1 step + 1 step) or (2 steps)

hints: The number of ways to reach step n only depends on how many ways there are to reach steps n-1 and n-2.
This is exactly the Fibonacci recurrence: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
You don't need an array — two running variables tracking the last two values are enough, giving O(1) space.

title: House Robber
description: Given an array representing money in houses along a street, find the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two directly adjacent houses.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 100
0 <= nums[i] <= 400

examples.explanation: Rob house 1 (1) and house 3 (3), total 4
Rob houses 1, 3, and 5 (2+9+1), total 12

hints: At each house, you have two choices: rob it (and skip the previous one) or skip it.
Define dp[i] = the max money obtainable considering houses 0..i: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
You only need the last two dp values at any point, so this can run in O(1) space.

title: Coin Change
description: Given an array of coin denominations and a target amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make that amount, or -1 if it's not possible.
constraints:
1 <= coins.length <= 12
1 <= coins[i] <= 2^31 - 1
0 <= amount <= 10^4

examples.explanation: 11 = 5 + 5 + 1, using 3 coins
3 cannot be made using only coin value 2

hints: A greedy 'always use the biggest coin' approach doesn't work for arbitrary denominations — think dynamic programming instead.
Define dp[a] = minimum coins to make amount a, with dp[0] = 0 and dp[a] = infinity initially.
For each amount from 1 to target, try every coin: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1) whenever a - coin >= 0 and dp[a - coin] is reachable.

title: Number of Islands
description: Given a 2D grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands, where an island is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
constraints:
1 <= grid rows, cols <= 300
Each cell is '0' or '1'

examples.explanation: One island in the top-left connected block, and one isolated island in the bottom-right
Two separate single-cell islands, not connected diagonally

hints: This is a connected-components problem on a grid — think of each land cell as a graph node connected to its land neighbors.
Scan every cell; whenever you find an unvisited '1', that's a new island — trigger a DFS or BFS to mark the whole connected region as visited.
Only count a new island each time you start a fresh flood-fill from an unvisited land cell; the flood-fill itself doesn't add to the count.

title: Course Schedule
description: Given the total number of courses and a list of prerequisite pairs, determine if it's possible to finish all courses — i.e., whether the prerequisite graph has no cycle.
constraints:
1 <= numCourses <= 2000
0 <= prerequisites.length <= 5000

examples.explanation: Take course 0 first, then course 1 — no cycle
Course 0 depends on 1 and 1 depends on 0 — a cycle, impossible to complete

hints: This is really asking: does the directed graph of prerequisites contain a cycle?
Use DFS with three states per node (unvisited, visiting, visited) — encountering a 'visiting' node again means a cycle.
Alternatively, use Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree 0; if you can't process all nodes this way, there's a cycle.

title: Clone Graph
description: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy (clone) of the entire graph.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [0, 100]
Each node has a unique value
The graph has no repeated edges or self-loops

examples.explanation: A deep clone with the same structure but entirely new node objects
A single node with no neighbors, cloned

hints: You need to avoid infinite loops since the graph can have cycles — track which nodes you've already cloned.
Use a hash map from original node to its clone; when you encounter a node you've already cloned, reuse that clone instead of creating a new one.
DFS (or BFS) from the given node, cloning each unvisited neighbor recursively and wiring up the clone's neighbor list to match the original's.

title: Single Number
description: Given a non-empty array where every element appears twice except for one, find that single one, in linear time and O(1) extra space.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 3*10^4
-3*10^4 <= nums[i] <= 3*10^4
Each element appears twice except for one

examples.explanation: 1 is the only element appearing once
4 appears once; 1 and 2 each appear twice

hints: A hash map counts occurrences in O(n) time and space — can you drop the extra space?
XOR has a useful property: a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a.
XOR every element together — all paired values cancel out, leaving only the single number.

title: Number of 1 Bits
description: Given a positive integer, return the number of set bits (1s) in its binary representation (Hamming weight).
constraints: The input is a 32-bit unsigned integer

examples.explanation: There are three 1 bits in 1011
Only one 1 bit

hints: Checking each of the 32 bits individually with a mask works but there's a faster trick.
n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit of n — think about why.
Repeatedly apply n = n & (n-1) and count how many times you can do it before n becomes 0; that's the number of set bits.

title: Counting Bits
description: Given an integer n, return an array of length n+1 where each index i holds the number of set bits in the binary representation of i.

examples.explanation: 0 has 0 bits, 1 has 1 bit, 2 (10) has 1 bit
Bit counts for 0 through 5

hints: Computing the bit count from scratch for every number is O(n log n) — you can reuse previous answers instead.
Every number i can be related to a smaller number you've already computed: i >> 1 (i with its last bit dropped).
dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — the count for i equals the count for i without its last bit, plus that last bit itself.

title: Jump Game
description: Given an array where each element represents your maximum jump length from that position, determine if you can reach the last index starting from index 0.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step from index 0 to 1, then 3 steps to the last index
You'll always land on index 3, whose max jump is 0, so index 4 is unreachable

hints: You don't need to try every jump combination — track the farthest index you can possibly reach so far.
Scan left to right, updating farthestReachable = max(farthestReachable, i + nums[i]) at each index i you can actually reach.
If at any point the current index i exceeds farthestReachable, you're stuck and can't proceed further.

title: Gas Station
description: There are n gas stations in a circle, each with a given amount of gas and a cost to travel to the next station. Determine the starting station index from which you can complete the full circuit, or -1 if impossible (guaranteed unique if it exists).
constraints:
n == gas.length == cost.length
1 <= n <= 10^5
0 <= gas[i], cost[i] <= 10^4

examples.explanation: Starting at station 3 lets you complete the full circuit without running out of gas
Total gas (9) is less than total cost (10), so no valid start exists

hints: First check feasibility: if total gas is less than total cost, no starting point works at all.
If a solution exists, it's unique — think about what disqualifies a starting point from being the answer.
Track a running tank total as you go around once; whenever the tank goes negative, no station up to and including the current one can be the start, so reset the candidate start to the next station.

title: Task Scheduler
description: Given an array of CPU tasks (represented by letters) and a cooldown period n between two identical tasks, find the minimum number of time units needed to finish all tasks (idle slots allowed).
constraints:
1 <= tasks.length <= 10^4
tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter
0 <= n <= 100

examples.explanation: One valid order: A B idle A B idle A B, total 8 units
No cooldown needed, so tasks run back to back with no idling

hints: The most frequent task determines the minimum spacing required — schedule around it first.
Count frequencies; let maxFreq be the highest count and maxCount be how many tasks share that highest frequency.
The answer is max(tasks.length, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + maxCount) — this formula accounts for the idle slots forced by the most frequent task(s).

title: Maximum Subarray
description: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.

examples.explanation: The subarray [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum, 6
A single element is trivially the max subarray

hints: Checking every subarray is O(n^2) — you want an O(n) pass instead.
At each position, decide: extend the current subarray, or start a fresh one here — whichever gives a larger sum.
currentSum = max(nums[i], currentSum + nums[i]); track the maximum currentSum seen across the whole scan — this is Kadane's algorithm.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
description: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product.

examples.explanation: The subarray [2,3] has the largest product, 6
The zero splits the array; the best product achievable is 0

hints: Unlike sums, a negative number can flip a very negative product into a very positive one — sums-based Kadane's doesn't directly work.
Track both the running maximum AND running minimum product ending at each position, since a negative number can turn the minimum into the new maximum.
At each step, compute candidates using the current number times the previous max, previous min, and the number alone, then update both running max and min accordingly.

title: Maximum Circular Subarray Sum
description: Given a circular integer array (the end connects back to the beginning), find the maximum possible sum of a non-empty subarray.

examples.explanation: The subarray [3] alone gives the maximum sum, 3, since wrapping around doesn't help here
Wrapping around: the two 5's at each end sum to 10

hints: There are two cases: the max subarray doesn't wrap around (regular Kadane's), or it does wrap around the array boundary.
A wrapping subarray's sum equals totalSum minus the MINIMUM subarray sum (the excluded middle part) — so compute both a max-subarray and a min-subarray pass.

Watch the edge case where all numbers are negative: the wrap-around case would incorrectly give an empty result, so fall back to the plain max-subarray answer whenever totalSum equals the minimum subarray sum.

title: Merge Intervals
description: Given an array of intervals, merge all overlapping (including touching) intervals and return the resulting non-overlapping intervals covering all the inputs.
constraints:
1 <= intervals.length <= 10^4
intervals[i].length == 2
0 <= starti <= endi <= 10^4

examples.explanation: [1,3] and [2,6] overlap and merge into [1,6]
[1,4] and [4,5] touch at 4 and merge into [1,5]

hints: Sorting the intervals by start time first makes overlaps easy to detect in a single left-to-right pass.
Keep a running 'merged' interval; if the next interval's start is <= the current merged interval's end, extend the end; otherwise close off the current merged interval and start a new one.
Don't forget to append the final merged interval after the loop ends.

title: Insert Interval
description: Given a set of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start time, insert a new interval into the set, merging as necessary to keep the intervals non-overlapping and sorted.
constraints:
0 <= intervals.length <= 10^4
intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order and non-overlapping

examples.explanation: [2,5] overlaps [1,3], merging into [1,5]; [6,9] stays separate
[4,8] overlaps [3,5], [6,7], and [8,10], merging them all into [3,10]

hints: Split the problem into three parts: intervals fully before the new one, overlapping intervals, and intervals fully after.
Add all intervals ending before the new interval starts as-is; then expand the new interval to absorb every interval that overlaps it; then add the rest as-is.
While merging overlapping intervals, keep updating the new interval's start (min) and end (max) as you absorb each one.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
description: Given an array of intervals, find the minimum number of intervals you need to remove so that the rest of the intervals are non-overlapping.
constraints:
1 <= intervals.length <= 10^5
intervals[i].length == 2
-5*10^4 <= starti < endi <= 5*10^4

examples.explanation: Removing [1,3] leaves [1,2],[2,3],[3,4], which are non-overlapping
Remove two of the three identical intervals, keeping just one

hints: This is equivalent to a classic scheduling problem: maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals you can KEEP, then subtract from the total.
Sort intervals by their END time, not start time — this is the key greedy insight.
Iterate through the sorted intervals, greedily keeping an interval whenever its start is >= the end of the last kept interval; count how many you keep, and the answer is total minus that count.

title: Unique Paths
description: A robot on an m x n grid starts at the top-left corner and can only move right or down. Return the number of unique paths to reach the bottom-right corner.

examples.explanation: There are 28 distinct right/down paths from top-left to bottom-right
Three distinct paths exist in a 3x2 grid

hints: Each cell's path count depends only on the cell above it and the cell to its left.
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], with the first row and first column all equal to 1 (only one way to reach them).
You can reduce this to a single 1D array updated in place, row by row, since each row only depends on the previous row.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
description: Given two strings, find the length of their longest common subsequence — a sequence that appears in both strings in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguous.
constraints:
1 <= text1.length, text2.length <= 1000
Both strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: The longest common subsequence is "ace", length 3
The entire string is a common subsequence

hints: Build a 2D table where dp[i][j] represents the LCS length using the first i characters of text1 and first j of text2.
If the characters at position i-1 and j-1 match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
If they don't match, dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — take the best result from dropping a character off either string.

title: Edit Distance
description: Given two strings, find the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or substitutions required to convert one string into the other.
constraints:
0 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 500
Both strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: horse -> rorse (replace h with r) -> rose (remove r) -> ros (remove e)
Five edits transform intention into execution

hints: This extends the Longest Common Subsequence idea — build a 2D table over prefixes of both strings.
dp[i][j] represents the minimum edits to convert the first i characters of word1 into the first j characters of word2.
If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i-1][j-1]) — covering insert, delete, and replace.

title: 0/1 Knapsack
description: Given weights and values of n items and a knapsack with a maximum weight capacity, determine the maximum total value achievable without exceeding the capacity. Each item can be used at most once.
constraints:
1 <= n <= 100
1 <= weights[i], values[i] <= 100
1 <= capacity <= 1000

examples.explanation: Taking items with weights 3 and 4 (values 4 and 5) gives value 9 within capacity 7
Only enough capacity for one item; the higher-value item worth 5 fits

hints: Since each item can only be used once, the order in which you consider items and update capacity matters.
dp[c] = max value achievable with capacity c; for each item, update dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - weight] + value).
To keep each item usable only once, iterate the capacity dimension from high to low when updating with a 1D array — this prevents reusing the same item multiple times within one pass.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
description: Given an array of positive integers, determine if it can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sums.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 200
1 <= nums[i] <= 100

examples.explanation: The array can be split into [1,5,5] and [11], both summing to 11
The total sum is 11, which is odd, so it can't be split into two equal halves

hints: If the total sum is odd, it's immediately impossible — two equal integer subsets can't sum to an odd total.
This reduces to: can you find a subset of nums that sums to exactly totalSum / 2? That's the classic 0/1 knapsack subset-sum problem.
Use a boolean dp array where dp[s] means 'sum s is achievable'; for each number, update dp from high to low to avoid reusing it twice.

title: Coin Change II
description: Given a target amount and an array of coin denominations, return the number of distinct combinations that make up that amount (order doesn't matter, unlimited supply of each coin).
constraints:
1 <= coins.length <= 300
1 <= coins[i] <= 5000
All coin values are unique
0 <= amount <= 5000

examples.explanation: No combination of 2's sums to 3

hints: This is an unbounded knapsack (coins can repeat) counting problem, not a minimization problem like the original Coin Change.
dp[a] = number of ways to make amount a; iterate coins on the OUTER loop and amounts on the inner loop, so combinations aren't counted as different orderings.
dp[a] += dp[a - coin] for each coin processed, going through amounts in increasing order for each coin — this allows reuse of the same coin.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Given an integer array, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing subsequence is [2,3,7,101] or [2,3,7,18], length 4
The longest increasing subsequence is [0,1,2,3], length 4

hints: A simple O(n^2) DP works: dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i.
dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i]; the answer is the max over all dp[i].
For an O(n log n) solution, maintain a 'tails' array of the smallest possible tail value for each subsequence length, using binary search to find where each new number fits.

title: Russian Doll Envelopes
description: Given pairs of envelope dimensions (width, height), find the maximum number of envelopes you can nest inside each other, where one envelope fits inside another only if both its width and height are strictly smaller.
constraints:
1 <= envelopes.length <= 10^5
envelopes[i].length == 2
1 <= widthi, heighti <= 10^5

examples.explanation: The best chain is [2,3] -> [5,4] -> [6,7], length 3
Identical envelopes can't nest inside each other, so the best chain is length 1

hints: This is really Longest Increasing Subsequence in disguise, but in two dimensions.
Sort envelopes by width ascending; for equal widths, sort by height DESCENDING — this prevents envelopes of the same width from being counted together in the LIS step.
After sorting, find the longest strictly increasing subsequence of the heights alone, using the O(n log n) LIS technique.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
description: Given an m x n integer matrix, find the length of the longest strictly increasing path, moving in any of the four cardinal directions at each step.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing path is [1,2,6,9], length 4
The longest increasing path is [3,4,5,6], length 4

hints: A plain DFS from every cell without memoization recomputes the same subpaths repeatedly — that's exponential.
Use DFS with memoization: memo[i][j] = the longest increasing path starting at cell (i,j), computed once and reused.
Recursively explore the four neighbors that have a strictly greater value than the current cell, take the max path length among them, add 1, and cache the result before returning.

title: Spiral Matrix
description: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements in spiral order (clockwise, starting from the top-left).

examples.explanation: Traversing clockwise starting from the top-left, spiraling inward
Spiral traversal of a non-square matrix

hints: Track four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right, and shrink them inward as you traverse each side.
Traverse right along the top row, down along the right column, left along the bottom row, and up along the left column, then move each boundary inward by one.
Watch for the edge cases where the matrix has only one row or one column left — check boundaries before each direction to avoid re-traversing or going out of bounds.

title: Rotate Image
description: Given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise, in place, without allocating another matrix.
constraints:
n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length
1 <= n <= 20
-1000 <= matrix[i][j] <= 1000

examples.explanation: Each element moves to its rotated position 90 degrees clockwise
A 2x2 matrix rotated 90 degrees clockwise

hints: Rotating 90 degrees clockwise can be decomposed into two simpler in-place operations.
First, transpose the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for all i < j).
Then, reverse each row — the combination of transpose plus row-reversal produces a 90-degree clockwise rotation.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
description: Given an m x n matrix where each row is sorted left to right and the first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row, determine if a target value exists in the matrix, in O(log(m*n)) time.

examples.explanation: 3 exists in the matrix at row 0
13 does not exist anywhere in the matrix

hints: Since the matrix rows and columns follow a strict sorted order overall, you can treat the whole matrix as one big sorted 1D array.
Use binary search directly over indices 0 to (m*n - 1), converting each mid index to a (row, col) pair using division and modulo by the number of columns.
mid -> row = mid / cols, col = mid % cols — then compare matrix[row][col] to the target as in ordinary binary search.

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
description: Given two strings, needle and haystack, return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack, or -1 if needle is not part of haystack.
constraints:
0 <= haystack.length, needle.length <= 5*10^4
Both strings consist of lowercase English characters

examples.explanation: "sad" occurs at index 0 and index 6; the first occurrence is at 0
"leeto" does not occur in "leetcode"

hints: A naive check-every-position approach is O(n*m) — for large inputs this is often too slow.
The KMP algorithm precomputes a 'failure function' (longest proper prefix that's also a suffix) for the needle, so matching never needs to backtrack in the haystack.
Build the failure table for needle first, then scan haystack once, using the table to skip ahead intelligently on a mismatch.

title: Repeated String Match
description: Given two strings a and b, return the minimum number of times a must be repeated so that b is a substring of the result, or -1 if it's never possible.
constraints:
1 <= a.length, b.length <= 10^4
Both strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Repeating a 3 times gives "abcdabcdabcd", which contains "cdabcdab"
b's characters never appear in a, so no repetition of a can ever contain b

hints: You only ever need to repeat a enough times so the repeated string's length is at least as long as b, plus possibly one more repetition.
Repeat a until its length is >= b's length, then check if b is a substring — if not, try one more repetition of a to handle b straddling the wrap-around point.
Use an efficient substring search (like KMP) for the containment check rather than a naive one, given the input sizes.

title: Shortest Palindrome
description: Given a string s, find the shortest palindrome you can form by adding characters only in front of s.
constraints:
0 <= s.length <= 5*10^4
s consists of lowercase English letters only

examples.explanation: Adding a single 'a' in front makes the whole string a palindrome
The longest palindromic prefix is just "a", so most of the reversed string must be prepended

hints: The key question is: what's the longest prefix of s that is itself a palindrome? Everything after that prefix needs to be mirrored and prepended.
Build a new string: s + a separator character (not in the alphabet) + reverse(s), then compute the KMP failure function on this combined string.
The value of the failure function at the very last position tells you the length of the longest palindromic prefix of s — prepend the reverse of everything after that prefix.

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
description: Implement a Trie class supporting insert(word), search(word) — checking if the exact word exists — and startsWith(prefix) — checking if any word begins with this prefix.
constraints:
1 <= word.length, prefix.length <= 2000
word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters
At most 3*10^4 calls total to insert, search, and startsWith

examples.input: insert("apple"), search("apple"), search("app"), startsWith("app"), insert("app"), search("app")
examples.explanation: After inserting "app" explicitly, search("app") becomes true
A single-character word inserted and found

hints: Each Trie node needs a way to reference its children (one per possible next character) and a flag marking whether a word ends there.
insert() walks the tree, creating child nodes for characters that don't exist yet, and marks the final node as 'end of word'.
search() and startsWith() both walk the tree following characters; search() additionally requires the final node to be marked 'end of word', while startsWith() doesn't.

title: Word Search II
description: Given an m x n grid of characters and a list of words, return all words from the list that can be formed by a sequence of adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically), using each cell at most once per word.
constraints:
1 <= m, n <= 12
1 <= words.length <= 3*10^4
1 <= words[i].length <= 10
All words[i] consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: "oath" and "eat" can be traced through adjacent cells; "pea" and "rain" cannot
"abcb" would require reusing the cell 'b' twice, which isn't allowed

hints: Searching for each word separately with DFS from every cell works but is slow when there are many words sharing prefixes.
Build a Trie from all the words first — this lets multiple word searches share the same DFS traversal of the board.

DFS from each cell, following the Trie alongside the board; when you land on a Trie node marked 'end of word', record that word, and prune the DFS whenever the current path no longer matches any Trie node.

title: Longest Word in Dictionary
description: Given an array of strings representing a dictionary, find the longest word that can be built one character at a time by other words in the dictionary (every prefix of the word must also exist in the dictionary). If there's a tie, return the lexicographically smallest one.
constraints:
1 <= words.length <= 1000
1 <= words[i].length <= 30
All words consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Each prefix (w, wo, wor, worl) also exists in the dictionary, so "world" is fully buildable
"apple" and "apply" are both fully buildable and the same length; "apple" is lexicographically smaller

hints: A word is 'buildable' if and only if every one of its prefixes also exists in the dictionary — this is naturally checked by walking a Trie.
Insert all words into a Trie, marking each node that corresponds to the end of an actual dictionary word.

Do a DFS (or BFS) from the root, only continuing into children whose node is marked as a valid word ending — this guarantees you only visit buildable words — and track the longest word found, with lexicographically smallest as the tiebreak.

title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
description: Design a class that, given an integer array, efficiently answers multiple queries for the sum of elements between two indices (inclusive), assuming the array doesn't change.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
-10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5
0 <= left <= right < nums.length
At most 10^4 calls to sumRange

examples.explanation: Sum from index 0 to 2 is -2+0+3=1, etc.
A single-element range sum

hints: Recomputing the sum for each query by scanning the range every time is O(n) per query — you can do better with preprocessing.
Build a prefix sum array where prefix[i] = sum of nums[0..i-1], computed once in O(n).
sumRange(left, right) = prefix[right+1] - prefix[left], answering each query in O(1) after the initial O(n) setup.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: Given an array of integers and an integer k, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.

examples.explanation: The subarrays [1,1] (indices 0-1) and [1,1] (indices 1-2) both sum to 2
The subarrays [1,2] and [3] both sum to 3

hints: Checking every subarray is O(n^2) — a running prefix sum combined with a hash map can do it in O(n).
If prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i] = k for some i < j, then the subarray between i+1 and j sums to k. Rearranged: prefixSum[i] = prefixSum[j] - k.

Keep a hash map of how many times each prefix sum value has occurred so far; at each step, add the count of (currentPrefixSum - k) to your running answer, then record the current prefix sum in the map.

title: Corporate Flight Bookings
description: There are n flights numbered 1 to n. Given a list of bookings, where each booking [first, last, seats] adds seats to every flight from first to last inclusive, return an array showing the total seats booked for each flight.
constraints:
1 <= n <= 2*10^4
1 <= bookings.length <= 2*10^4
1 <= firsti <= lasti <= n
1 <= seatsi <= 10^4

examples.explanation: Flight 2 gets seats from all three bookings: 10+20+25=55
Flight 2 gets seats from both bookings: 10+15=25

hints: Directly adding seats to every flight in each range is O(bookings * range length), which can be slow for large ranges.
Use a difference array: for each booking, add seats at index (first-1) and subtract seats at index last (if within bounds).
After processing all bookings, compute the running prefix sum of the difference array — that gives you the final seat count for every flight in one O(n) pass.

title: Greatest Common Divisor of Two Numbers
description: Given two positive integers, find their greatest common divisor (GCD) — the largest number that divides both without a remainder.

examples.explanation: 6 is the largest number dividing both 12 and 18
17 is prime and shares no common factor with 5 other than 1

hints: Checking every number up to min(a, b) is O(min(a,b)) — far too slow for large inputs.
The Euclidean algorithm relies on the fact that gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b).
Repeatedly replace (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b becomes 0 — at that point, a is the GCD. This runs in O(log(min(a,b))) time.

title: Least Common Multiple of an Array
description: Given an array of positive integers, find the least common multiple (LCM) of all of them.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 20
1 <= nums[i] <= 10^4

examples.explanation: 12 is the smallest number divisible by both 4 and 6
60 is the smallest number divisible by 3, 4, and 5

hints: The LCM of two numbers relates directly to their GCD: lcm(a, b) = (a * b) / gcd(a, b).
Extend this pairwise: fold the LCM computation across the array, using the running LCM combined with the next number each time.
Watch for integer overflow when multiplying large numbers before dividing — dividing by the GCD first (a / gcd(a,b) * b) can help avoid it.

title: Nth Ugly Number
description: An ugly number is a positive integer whose prime factors are limited to 2, 3, and 5. Given an integer n, return the nth ugly number (1 is conventionally treated as the first ugly number).

examples.explanation: The first 10 ugly numbers are 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12
1 has no prime factors, so it's the first ugly number by convention

hints: Checking every integer for 'ugliness' by repeatedly dividing out 2, 3, and 5 works but can be slow for larger n.
Every ugly number (after 1) is generated by multiplying a smaller ugly number by 2, 3, or 5 — build the sequence rather than checking each candidate.

Maintain three pointers into the growing ugly-number list, one for each of the multipliers 2, 3, and 5; at each step, take the minimum of the three candidate products as the next ugly number, and advance whichever pointer(s) produced that minimum.

title: Count Primes
description: Given an integer n, return the number of prime numbers strictly less than n.

examples.explanation: There are 4 primes less than 10: 2, 3, 5, 7
No primes less than 0

hints: Checking primality of each number individually (trial division up to its square root) is O(n * sqrt(n)) overall — too slow for large n.
The Sieve of Eratosthenes marks composites in bulk: starting from 2, mark all multiples of each prime as not-prime.

You only need to sieve starting multiples from p*p onward (smaller multiples of p were already marked by smaller primes), and you only need to sieve primes up to sqrt(n) before all remaining unmarked numbers are guaranteed prime.

title: Four Divisors
description: Given an array of integers, for every number that has exactly four divisors, add up those four divisors; return the total sum across all such numbers (0 if none qualify).
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 10^4
1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5

examples.explanation: 21 has divisors 1,3,7,21 (sum 32); 4 has divisors 1,2,4 (only 3, doesn't qualify); 7 has divisors 1,7 (only 2, doesn't qualify)
Both 21's qualify, contributing 32 each

hints: Finding all divisors of a number by checking every value up to n is O(n) per number — you can do it in O(sqrt(n)).
For each number, check divisors up to its square root; each divisor d found also gives you a paired divisor n/d.
Collect all divisor pairs into a set (to avoid double-counting perfect squares), and only sum them if the total count is exactly 4.

title: Prime Factorization Queries
description: Given an integer n, precompute a structure that lets you quickly find the smallest prime factor of any number from 1 to n, then use it to return the full prime factorization of a given query number q (1 <= q <= n).

examples.explanation: 97 is prime, so its only prime factor is itself

hints: A modified sieve can record, for every number up to n, its smallest prime factor (SPF) instead of just a true/false 'is prime' flag.
Build the SPF array: for each prime p found during the sieve, mark SPF[multiple] = p for every unmarked multiple of p.
To factorize q, repeatedly divide q by SPF[q] and record that factor, until q becomes 1 — each factorization takes O(log q) steps total since q shrinks geometrically.

title: Modular Exponentiation
description: Given a base, an exponent, and a modulus, compute (base ^ exponent) % modulus efficiently, without ever computing the full power directly.
constraints:
1 <= base, modulus <= 10^9
0 <= exponent <= 10^9

examples.explanation: Any number to the power 0 is 1, and 1 % 7 = 1

hints: Computing base^exponent directly then taking the modulus overflows for large exponents — you need to reduce modulo at every step.
Use fast (binary) exponentiation: exponentiation by squaring reduces the number of multiplications from O(exponent) to O(log exponent).
At each step, square the base (mod modulus) and halve the exponent; if the exponent is odd, multiply the running result by the current base (mod modulus) before squaring.

title: Count of Subarrays with Sum Divisible by K
description: Given an array of integers and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.

examples.explanation: There are 7 subarrays whose sum is a multiple of 5
The only subarray [5] has sum 5, not divisible by 9

hints: This extends 'Subarray Sum Equals K' but uses remainders instead of exact sums, since you're checking divisibility, not an exact value.
Two prefix sums with the SAME remainder when divided by k mean the subarray between them has a sum divisible by k.

In many languages the modulo of a negative number can be negative — normalize it into the range [0, k-1] by adding k and taking modulo k again, then count occurrences of each remainder using a hash map, similar to the exact-sum version.

title: Count Good Numbers
description: A digit string is 'good' if digits at even indices are even (0,2,4,6,8) and digits at odd indices are prime (2,3,5,7). Given an integer n, return the number of good digit strings of length n, modulo 10^9 + 7.

examples.explanation: There are 5 valid single-digit good strings: 0,2,4,6,8 (only the even-index rule applies)
There are 400 good strings of length 4, computed as 5^2 * 4^2 mod (10^9+7)

hints: Count how many even-indexed positions there are (ceil(n/2), each with 5 choices) and how many odd-indexed positions there are (floor(n/2), each with 4 choices).
The total count is 5^(number of even positions) * 4^(number of odd positions), all taken modulo 10^9 + 7.
Since n can be astronomically large, you must use fast modular exponentiation to compute each power efficiently — computing it directly would never finish.

title: Pascal's Triangle
description: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows of Pascal's triangle, where each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.
constraints: 1 <= numRows <= 30

examples.explanation: Each row starts and ends with 1, with interior values being the sum of the two above
A single row containing just 1

hints: Each row can be built directly from the previous row without recomputing factorials or combinations from scratch.
Start each row with a 1, then for each interior position, sum the two values directly above it from the previous row, and end with a 1.
Row i, position j is equivalent to the binomial coefficient C(i, j), which is exactly what this row-by-row summation computes.

title: Unique Paths II (with Obstacles)
description: A robot on an m x n grid (containing some obstacles marked 1, open cells marked 0) starts at the top-left and can only move right or down. Return the number of unique paths to the bottom-right, avoiding obstacles.
constraints:
m == obstacleGrid.length
n == obstacleGrid[i].length
1 <= m, n <= 100
obstacleGrid[i][j] is 0 or 1

examples.explanation: There are 2 valid paths avoiding the obstacle in the middle
Only one valid path exists, going straight down then right

hints: Without obstacles this is a pure combinatorics problem (count paths using binomial coefficients), but obstacles break that clean formula.
Fall back to dynamic programming: dp[i][j] = number of ways to reach cell (i,j), which is 0 if that cell is an obstacle.
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] when the cell is open; initialize the first row and column carefully, since an obstacle anywhere in them blocks all cells after it in that row/column.

title: Permutation Sequence
description: Given n and k, return the kth permutation sequence of the numbers 1 to n, in lexicographic order (without generating all permutations).

examples.explanation: The permutations of [1,2,3] in order are 123,132,213,231,312,321 — the 3rd one is 213
The 9th permutation of [1,2,3,4] in lexicographic order is 2314

hints: Generating all n! permutations and picking the kth is far too slow for larger n — use the structure of the factorial number system instead.
There are (n-1)! permutations starting with each possible first digit; you can determine the first digit directly by dividing (k-1) by (n-1)!.

Repeat this process for each remaining position: at each step, pick the next available digit using (remaining index) / (remaining factorial), remove that digit from the pool, and reduce the index using the remainder of that division.

title: Daily Temperatures
description: Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array where each element is the number of days you'd have to wait for a warmer temperature; if there's no future warmer day, put 0.
constraints:
1 <= temperatures.length <= 10^5
30 <= temperatures[i] <= 100

examples.explanation: For day 0 (73), the next warmer day is day 1 (74), 1 day away
Each day is immediately followed by a warmer one, except the last

hints: A brute-force scan-ahead from every day is O(n^2) in the worst case — a monotonic stack gets this to O(n).
Maintain a stack of indices whose temperatures are still 'waiting' for a warmer day, keeping temperatures in decreasing order from bottom to top.

When you encounter a temperature warmer than the one at the top of the stack, pop it and record the day difference as the answer for that popped index; repeat until the stack top is no longer smaller (or empty), then push the current index.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: Given an array of bar heights representing a histogram (each bar has width 1), find the area of the largest rectangle that can be formed within the histogram.
constraints:
1 <= heights.length <= 10^5
0 <= heights[i] <= 10^4

examples.explanation: The largest rectangle has height 5 and width 2 (bars at indices 2-3), giving area 10
The largest rectangle uses just the bar of height 4, area 4

hints: For each bar, the largest rectangle using that bar's height extends as far left and right as neighboring bars are at least as tall — brute-force checking this for every bar is O(n^2).
Use a monotonic increasing stack of indices; when you find a bar shorter than the one at the top of the stack, that's the signal the top bar's rectangle is now fully bounded.
When popping a bar from the stack, its rectangle's width is determined by the current index and the new stack top (after popping) — compute and track the max area at each pop.

title: Sum of Subarray Minimums
description: Given an array of integers, find the sum of min(subarray) over all contiguous subarrays, modulo 10^9 + 7.

examples.explanation: Summing the minimums of all 10 possible subarrays gives 17
The sum of all subarray minimums modulo 10^9+7 is 444

hints: Checking every subarray directly is O(n^2) or worse — think about each element's individual contribution instead.
For each element, figure out how many subarrays it is the MINIMUM of — that count times its value contributes to the total sum.

Use a monotonic increasing stack to find, for each element, the distance to the nearest smaller element on the left and on the right; multiply these two distances together to get the number of subarrays where this element is the minimum.

title: Number of Provinces
description: Given an n x n adjacency matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means cities i and j are directly connected, return the total number of provinces (a province is a group of directly or indirectly connected cities).
constraints:
1 <= n <= 200
isConnected[i][j] is 1 or 0
isConnected[i][i] == 1
isConnected[i][j] == isConnected[j][i]

examples.explanation: Cities 0 and 1 form one province; city 2 forms its own province
No cities are connected, so each is its own province

hints: This is a connected-components problem, which Union-Find solves cleanly without needing a full graph traversal per component.
Initialize each city as its own parent; for every pair (i,j) marked connected, union them together.
After processing all pairs, count the number of distinct root parents remaining — that's the number of provinces.

title: Redundant Connection
description: Given a graph that started as a tree with n nodes but has one extra edge added (creating exactly one cycle), find the edge that can be removed to restore it to a tree. If multiple answers exist, return the one that appears last in the input.
constraints:
n == edges.length
3 <= n <= 1000
Each edge is a pair of distinct integers from 1 to n

examples.explanation: Removing edge [2,3] restores the tree; it's the redundant edge that closes the cycle
[1,4] is the edge that closes the cycle 1-2-3-4-1

hints: A cycle forms exactly when you try to union two nodes that are already in the same connected component.
Process edges in order, using Union-Find; for each edge, check if the two endpoints already share the same root before unioning.

The first edge where both endpoints are already connected (same root) is the redundant one — since edges are processed in input order, this naturally gives you the one that appears last among the cycle-closing edges.

title: Accounts Merge
description: Given a list of accounts, where each account has a name and a list of emails, merge accounts that share at least one email (belonging to the same person), and return the merged accounts with sorted emails.
constraints:
1 <= accounts.length <= 1000
2 <= accounts[i].length <= 10
1 <= accounts[i][j].length <= 30

examples.explanation: The first and third John accounts share "johnsmith@mail.com" and get merged; the second John account has no shared email so stays separate
A single account with no overlaps stays as-is

hints: Think of every email as a node, and each account as a set of edges connecting its emails together.
Use Union-Find: for each account, union all its emails together under one representative.

After unioning, group emails by their root parent, then for each group look up any account containing one of those emails to recover the associated name, and output the sorted merged email list per group.

title: Course Schedule II
description: Given numCourses and a list of prerequisite pairs, return a valid ordering of courses that satisfies all prerequisites, or an empty array if it's impossible.
constraints:
1 <= numCourses <= 2000
0 <= prerequisites.length <= numCourses * (numCourses - 1)

examples.explanation: Course 0 must be taken before course 1
Multiple valid orderings exist since 1 and 2 don't depend on each other

hints: This is exactly Course Schedule (cycle detection) but you also need to record a valid order, not just true/false.
Use Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly process nodes with in-degree 0, adding them to the result and decrementing the in-degree of their neighbors.
If your result list ends up shorter than numCourses, a cycle exists somewhere and no valid ordering is possible — return an empty array in that case.

title: Alien Dictionary
description: Given a sorted list of words from an alien language using some subset of the English alphabet, derive the order of characters used in that language, or return an empty string if the order is invalid or unresolvably ambiguous.
constraints:
1 <= words.length <= 100
1 <= words[i].length <= 100
All characters are lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Comparing adjacent words letter by letter reveals the ordering w<e, r<t, e<r, t<f
z appearing before x and also after x is a contradiction, so no valid order exists

hints: Compare each pair of adjacent words to find the first differing character — that gives you a 'comes before' relationship between two letters, forming a directed graph edge.
Build a graph of these letter-ordering constraints, then this becomes a topological sort problem over the alphabet used.

Watch for two invalid cases: a cycle in the constraint graph (contradictory ordering), and a word that is a longer prefix appearing before its own shorter prefix (like "abc" before "ab"), which is invalid regardless of letter ordering.

title: Minimum Height Trees
description: Given a tree with n nodes (as an undirected graph with n-1 edges), find all root nodes that minimize the height of the resulting rooted tree, and return them.
constraints:
1 <= n <= 2*10^4
edges.length == n - 1
The input is guaranteed to be a valid tree

examples.explanation: Rooting the tree at node 1 gives the smallest possible height
Rooting at either 3 or 4 gives the same minimal height

hints: The answer is always at most 2 nodes, and they lie at the 'center' of the tree's longest path.
Think of this like peeling layers off an onion: repeatedly remove all current leaf nodes (degree 1), layer by layer.
The last remaining node(s) after repeatedly stripping leaves — using a queue similar to topological sort / Kahn's algorithm on degree counts — are the answer.

title: Network Delay Time
description: Given a network of n nodes and a list of weighted directed edges (travel times), find the minimum time for a signal sent from a given node k to reach all n nodes. Return -1 if it's impossible for all nodes to receive the signal.

examples.explanation: From node 2, the farthest node (4) takes 2 time units to reach
Node 2 receives the signal after 1 time unit

hints: This is a classic single-source shortest path problem with non-negative weights — a strong signal to use Dijkstra's algorithm.
Use a min-heap (priority queue) that always processes the currently-closest unvisited node next, relaxing its outgoing edges.
After running Dijkstra's from node k, the answer is the maximum distance among all nodes; if any node is still unreachable (infinite distance), return -1.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
description: Given n cities connected by weighted directed flights, and a source, destination, and maximum number of stops k, find the cheapest price to travel from source to destination using at most k stops. Return -1 if there's no valid route.
constraints:
1 <= n <= 100
0 <= flights.length <= (n * (n-1) / 2)
0 <= src, dst, k < n

examples.explanation: With at most 1 stop, the route 0->1->3 costs 100+600=700
With at most 1 stop, the route 0->1->2 costs 100+100=200, cheaper than the direct flight

hints: Standard Dijkstra's doesn't directly respect a hard limit on the NUMBER of stops, since it only tracks total cost — you need to track stops too.
Bellman-Ford is naturally suited here: relax all edges repeatedly, but limit the number of relaxation rounds to (k+1), matching at most k stops.
Use a temporary copy of distances at the start of each round so you don't use edges already relaxed within the same round, which would incorrectly allow more stops than the round number represents.

title: Find the City With the Smallest Number of Neighbors at a Threshold Distance
description: Given n cities connected by weighted undirected edges and a distance threshold, find the city that has the smallest number of other cities reachable within the threshold distance (using the shortest path). If there's a tie, return the city with the greatest index.
constraints:
2 <= n <= 100
1 <= edges.length <= n * (n-1) / 2
1 <= weight <= 10^4

examples.explanation: City 3 can reach the fewest other cities within distance 4
City 0 has the fewest reachable neighbors within distance 2

hints: Since you need all-pairs shortest distances (not just from one source), Floyd-Warshall is a natural fit for this graph size.
Floyd-Warshall computes shortest distances between every pair of nodes in O(n^3) by considering each node as a potential intermediate point in a path.

After computing the full distance matrix, count how many cities each city can reach within the threshold, then pick the city with the fewest reachable cities, breaking ties by choosing the largest index.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
description: Given the coordinates of n points on a 2D plane, find the minimum total cost to connect all points, where the cost between two points is their Manhattan distance.
constraints:
1 <= points.length <= 1000
-10^6 <= xi, yi <= 10^6

examples.explanation: The minimum spanning tree connecting all 5 points has total Manhattan-distance cost 20
Connecting all 3 points with minimum total Manhattan distance costs 18

hints: Every pair of points can be an edge with weight equal to their Manhattan distance — this is a complete graph, and you want its minimum spanning tree.
Prim's algorithm works well here: grow the tree one point at a time, always adding the cheapest edge that connects a new point to the existing tree.
Alternatively, use Kruskal's algorithm with Union-Find: generate all O(n^2) edges, sort them by weight, and greedily add edges that don't create a cycle until all points are connected.

title: Connecting Cities With Minimum Cost
description: Given n cities and a list of weighted connections between some pairs of cities, find the minimum total cost to connect all cities together, or -1 if it's impossible.
constraints:
1 <= n <= 10^4
1 <= connections.length <= 10^4
Each connection is [city1, city2, cost]

examples.explanation: Using edges (2,3,1) and (1,2,5), total cost is 6, connecting all 3 cities
Cities {1,2} and {3,4} form two separate disconnected groups

hints: This is a direct application of finding a minimum spanning tree — with the twist that the graph might not be fully connected to begin with.
Sort all connections by cost, then use Union-Find to greedily add the cheapest connections that don't create a cycle (Kruskal's algorithm).
After processing all connections, check if exactly n-1 edges were added (forming a spanning tree over n cities) — if fewer were added, some cities remain disconnected, so return -1.

title: Optimize Water Distribution in a Village
description: Given n houses, the cost to build a well directly at each house, and pipe costs between pairs of houses, find the minimum total cost to supply water to every house (either via a well or a connected pipe network).
constraints:
1 <= n <= 10^4
wells.length == n
0 <= pipes.length <= 10^5
Each pipe is [house1, house2, cost]

examples.explanation: Build a well at house 1 (cost 1), then connect pipes 1-2 and 2-3 (cost 1 each), total 3
Build one well (cost 1) and one connecting pipe (cost 1), total 2

hints: Think of 'building a well at house i' as equivalent to connecting house i to a single imaginary 'virtual node 0' with an edge weight equal to the well's cost.
With this trick, the problem becomes a standard minimum spanning tree problem over n+1 nodes (the virtual node plus all houses).
Combine the well-costs (as edges to the virtual node) with the pipe-costs into one edge list, sort by cost, and run Kruskal's algorithm with Union-Find to find the minimum spanning tree total.

title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
description: Given an integer array, return a new array where each element counts how many numbers to its right are smaller than it.

examples.explanation: To the right of 5: 2 and 1 are smaller (2); to the right of 2: only 1 is smaller (1); to the right of 6: only 1 is smaller (1); nothing to the right of 1 (0)
No elements to the right

hints: A brute-force O(n^2) comparison works but is too slow for large inputs.

Use a modified merge sort: while merging two sorted halves, track how many elements from the right half get merged in before each element from the left half — that count is exactly how many smaller elements appear after it.
Track original indices alongside values as you sort, so counts can be attributed back to the correct original position after the divide-and-conquer merge completes.

title: Different Ways to Add Parentheses
