description: Given a string of numbers and operators (+, -, *), return all possible results from computing all different ways to group the numbers and operators via parentheses.
constraints:
1 <= expression.length <= 20
expression consists of digits and the operators + - *
All intermediate results fit in a 32-bit integer

examples.explanation: ((2-1)-1) = 0 and (2-(1-1)) = 2 are the two distinct results
Five distinct groupings produce these five values

hints: Every operator in the expression is a potential 'split point' that divides the expression into a left and right sub-expression.
Recursively compute all possible results for the left part and all possible results for the right part around each operator, then combine every pair using that operator.
Memoize results for repeated sub-expressions to avoid redundant recomputation, since the same substring can appear multiple times during the recursive splitting.

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
description: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the two arrays combined, in O(log(m+n)) time.

examples.explanation: The merged array is [1,2,3], whose median is 2
The merged array is [1,2,3,4], whose median is (2+3)/2 = 2.5

hints: Merging both arrays and finding the median directly is O(m+n) — the log(m+n) requirement signals you need binary search instead.
Binary search on the smaller array to find a 'partition point' such that all elements on the left of both partitions combined are less than or equal to all elements on the right.
Once you find a valid partition (left max <= right min on both sides), the median is derived directly from the boundary elements around the partition, handling odd vs even total length separately.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
description: Given a string, return the longest substring that is a palindrome.
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 1000
s consists of digits and English letters

examples.explanation: Both "bab" and "aba" are valid answers, length 3
"bb" is the longest palindromic substring, length 2

hints: A brute-force check of every substring is O(n^3) — 'expand around center' brings this down to O(n^2).
For each position, treat it as a potential palindrome center and expand outward in both directions, checking both odd-length and even-length centers.
For an O(n) solution, use Manacher's algorithm, which cleverly reuses previously computed palindrome radii to avoid redundant expansion work.

title: Palindromic Substrings
description: Given a string, return the total number of palindromic substrings it contains (substrings at different positions are counted separately, even if identical).
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 1000
s consists of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Three palindromic substrings: "a", "b", "c"
Six palindromic substrings: "a", "a", "a", "aa", "aa", "aaa"

hints: Every single character is trivially a palindrome — start your count there.
Use the same 'expand around center' technique as Longest Palindromic Substring, but instead of tracking the longest one, count every successful expansion.
There are 2n-1 possible centers (n single-character centers and n-1 between-character centers for even-length palindromes) — expand from each and count all valid expansions.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
description: Given a string, partition it such that every substring in the partition is a palindrome, and return all possible palindrome partitionings.
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 16
s consists of lowercase English letters only

examples.explanation: Both partitionings split "aab" entirely into palindromic pieces
A single character is trivially a palindrome and the only partitioning

hints: This is a backtracking problem: at each position, try every possible palindromic prefix as the next partition piece.
Precompute (or check on the fly) whether each substring is a palindrome, ideally using a 2D dp table dp[i][j] = 'is s[i..j] a palindrome' to avoid redundant checks.
Backtrack from the current start index: for each end index where s[start..end] is a palindrome, add it to the current partition, recurse from end+1, then remove it before trying the next option.

title: Valid Anagram
description: Given two strings, determine if the second string is an anagram of the first (same characters, same frequencies, possibly different order).
constraints:
1 <= s.length, t.length <= 5*10^4
Both strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: t contains exactly the same letters as s, just rearranged
t contains a 'c' which doesn't appear in s

hints: If the two strings have different lengths, they can't possibly be anagrams — check that first as a quick shortcut.
Count the frequency of each character in both strings and compare the counts, or sort both strings and compare directly.
A single frequency array of size 26 (for lowercase letters), incremented for s and decremented for t, should end up all zeros if and only if the strings are anagrams.

title: Find All Anagrams in a String
description: Given a string s and a string p, return the starting indices of all substrings in s that are anagrams of p.
constraints:
1 <= s.length, p.length <= 3*10^4
Both strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: The substring starting at index 0 ("cba") and index 6 ("bac") are both anagrams of "abc"
Substrings at indices 0, 1, and 2 are all anagrams of "ab"

hints: Checking every window of length p.length by sorting or full frequency comparison is O(n * k) — a sliding window can make this O(n).
Maintain a frequency count of characters in the current window of s and compare it to the frequency count of p as the window slides.

Instead of comparing full frequency maps at every position, maintain a running count of how many character frequencies currently 'match' between the window and p, updating it incrementally as the window slides by one character.

title: Group Shifted Strings
description: Given an array of strings, group together strings that can be obtained from one another by shifting each letter by a consistent amount (wrapping z to a). Return the groups in any order.
constraints:
1 <= strings.length <= 200
1 <= strings[i].length <= 50
All strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Strings with the same pattern of consecutive letter differences (with wraparound) are grouped together
A single string forms its own group

hints: Two strings belong to the same group exactly when the difference between consecutive characters (mod 26, to handle wraparound) is identical throughout both strings.
For each string, compute a 'shift signature': the sequence of differences between each character and the next, normalized with modulo 26 to handle negative wraparound (like z to a).
Use this signature as a hash map key, and group all strings sharing the same signature together.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
description: Given a string, find the length of the longest subsequence that is a palindrome (not necessarily contiguous).
constraints:
1 <= s.length <= 1000
s consists only of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: One longest palindromic subsequence is "bbbb", length 4
One longest palindromic subsequence is "bb", length 2

hints: This can be reframed as the Longest Common Subsequence between the string and its own reverse — but a direct DP is also natural.
Define dp[i][j] = length of the longest palindromic subsequence within s[i..j].
If s[i] == s[j], dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j-1] + 2; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]) — fill the table by increasing substring length.

title: Distinct Subsequences
description: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t.
constraints:
1 <= s.length, t.length <= 1000
Both strings consist of English letters

examples.explanation: There are 3 distinct ways to pick characters from s to spell "rabbit"
There are 5 distinct ways to select characters from s to spell "bag"

hints: Build a 2D table dp[i][j] = number of ways to form the first j characters of t using the first i characters of s.
If s[i-1] == t[j-1], you have two choices: use s[i-1] to match t[j-1] (dp[i-1][j-1] ways), or skip s[i-1] entirely (dp[i-1][j] ways) — sum both.
If the characters don't match, you can only skip s[i-1], so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]; initialize dp[i][0] = 1 for all i, since there's exactly one way to form an empty string (skip everything).

title: Wildcard Matching
description: Given a string s and a pattern p containing the wildcards '?' (matches any single character) and '*' (matches any sequence of characters, including none), determine if the pattern matches the entire string.
constraints:
0 <= s.length, p.length <= 2000
s consists of lowercase English letters
p consists of lowercase English letters, '?', or '*'

examples.explanation: "a" cannot match the entire string "aa"
'?' matches 'c', but 'a' does not match 'b'

hints: Build a 2D table dp[i][j] = whether the first i characters of s match the first j characters of p.

If p[j-1] is '?' or matches s[i-1] exactly, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; if p[j-1] is '*', it can match zero characters (dp[i][j-1]) or one more character (dp[i-1][j]) — dp[i][j] is true if either is true.
Initialize carefully: dp[0][0] = true (empty matches empty), and dp[0][j] for a pattern of all leading '*' characters can still be true, since '*' can match zero characters.

title: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
description: Given an array of integers and an integer k, determine whether it's possible to divide the array into k non-empty subsets with equal sums.
constraints:
1 <= k <= nums.length <= 16
1 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
The frequency of each element is in the range [1, 4]

examples.explanation: The array can be split into 4 subsets each summing to 5: (5), (1,4), (2,3), (2,3)
The total sum 10 is not divisible by 3, so equal subsets are impossible

hints: First check divisibility: if the total sum isn't divisible by k, it's immediately impossible.
With up to 16 elements, you can represent which elements have been 'used' as a bitmask (2^16 possible states), enabling a DP over subsets.

dp[mask] = true if the elements represented by mask can be perfectly partitioned into complete subsets summing to the target; try adding each unused element to the current subset and recurse, resetting the running subset sum to 0 whenever it hits the target.

title: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
description: Given an undirected connected graph, find the length of the shortest path that visits every node at least once, starting from any node and ending anywhere.
constraints:
n == graph.length
1 <= n <= 12
0 <= graph[i].length < n

examples.explanation: One valid shortest path is [1,0,2,0,3], visiting all 4 nodes with 4 edges traversed
A path visiting all 5 nodes with 4 edges exists

hints: With n up to 12, the 'set of nodes visited so far' can be represented as a bitmask with up to 2^12 states.

Use BFS over states of (current node, visited-mask), where each state transition moves to a neighbor and updates the mask — the first time you reach a state where the mask includes all nodes gives the shortest path length.
Start the BFS from every node simultaneously (each as its own starting state with only itself marked visited), since the path can begin anywhere.

title: Minimum Cost to Connect Two Groups of Points
description: Given the cost matrix between two groups of points (size1 x size2), connect every point in the first group to at least one point in the second group and vice versa, minimizing total connection cost.
constraints:
size1 == cost.length
size2 == cost[i].length
1 <= size1, size2 <= 12
0 <= cost[i][j] <= 100

examples.explanation: Connecting point 0 of group1 to point 0 of group2 (cost 15) and point 1 to point 1 (cost 2) gives total 17
The minimum total connection cost achievable is 4

hints: Since size2 is small (up to 12), represent which points in group2 have been connected so far as a bitmask.
Define dp[i][mask] = minimum cost to connect the first i points of group1, where mask tracks which group2 points have been used at least once so far.

For each point in group1, try connecting it to every point in group2 (updating the mask), and after processing all of group1, add the minimum cost to connect any still-unconnected group2 points individually to their cheapest match.

title: House Robber III
description: Given the root of a binary tree representing houses, where directly connected houses (parent and child) cannot both be robbed, find the maximum amount of money that can be robbed without alerting the police.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4]
0 <= Node.val <= 10^4

examples.explanation: Robbing nodes 3, 3, and 1 (avoiding the directly connected 2) gives total 3+3+1=7
Robbing nodes 4 and 5 gives total 9, which is the best achievable

hints: This is House Robber but on a tree instead of a line — you still can't rob two directly connected nodes.
For each node, compute two values via post-order DFS: the best result if this node IS robbed, and the best result if it is NOT robbed.
If robbed: node.val + sum of (not-robbed values) of both children. If not robbed: sum of max(robbed, not-robbed) of both children. The final answer is the max of both values at the root.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
description: Given the root of a binary tree, find the maximum path sum, where a path is any non-empty sequence of nodes connected by edges (doesn't need to pass through the root, and each node can appear at most once).
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [1, 3*10^4]
-1000 <= Node.val <= 1000

examples.explanation: The path 2 -> 1 -> 3 has the maximum sum, 6
The path 15 -> 20 -> 7 has the maximum sum, 42

hints: For each node, the maximum path sum 'through' it (as the highest point of the path) combines its value with the best contributions from both its left and right subtrees.
But the value a node can CONTRIBUTE upward to its parent can only include one side — either the left branch or the right branch, not both, since a path can't branch.

Recursively compute, for each node, the max single-branch contribution it can offer upward (clamped at 0 if negative, since you can just not extend through a negative branch), while separately tracking the best 'through this node' sum (using both branches) as a global running maximum.

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length (in number of edges) of the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. This path may or may not pass through the root.
constraints:
The number of nodes is in the range [1, 10^4]
-100 <= Node.val <= 100

examples.explanation: The longest path is [4,2,1,3] (or [5,2,1,3]), which has 3 edges
The only path is between the two nodes, length 1

hints: The diameter through any given node equals the sum of the heights of its left and right subtrees.
Use post-order DFS: compute the height of each subtree (1 + max(left height, right height)) while, at each node, checking if leftHeight + rightHeight beats the best diameter found so far.
Track the maximum diameter as a variable updated during the height-computation recursion, rather than computing heights and diameters in two separate passes — this keeps the whole algorithm O(n).

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
description: Design a class that supports updating a value at a given index and querying the sum of elements between two indices (inclusive), both efficiently — better than O(n) per operation.
constraints:
1 <= nums.length <= 3*10^4
-100 <= nums[i] <= 100
0 <= index < nums.length
0 <= left <= right < nums.length
At most 3*10^4 calls to update and sumRange combined

examples.explanation: Initial sum 0-2 is 1+3+5=9; after updating index 1 to value 2, the new sum 0-2 is 1+2+5=8
After updating index 4 to 6, sum from index 2 to 4 is 5+7+6=18

hints: A prefix-sum array (like the immutable version) makes updates O(n) since every prefix after the changed index must be recomputed — you need a structure that supports both operations efficiently.
A Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) or a Segment Tree both support point updates and range sum queries in O(log n) each.

With a Fenwick Tree, updates propagate through indices by repeatedly adding the lowest set bit, and prefix sum queries accumulate by repeatedly removing the lowest set bit — both O(log n) per operation.

title: Count of Range Sum
description: Given an integer array and a lower and upper bound, return the number of range sums that lie within [lower, upper] inclusive (a range sum is the sum of elements between two indices, inclusive).

examples.explanation: Three range sums fall in [-2,2]: [-2], [-1], and [-2,5,-1] which sums to 2
The single range sum [0] falls within [0,0]

hints: Checking all O(n^2) range sums directly is too slow for large inputs — this again reduces to counting valid prefix-sum pairs.
A range sum between indices i+1 and j equals prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i], so you need to count pairs (i,j) where lower <= prefixSum[j] - prefixSum[i] <= upper.

A Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) over the compressed/sorted prefix sum values, or a modified merge sort similar to 'Count of Smaller Numbers After Self', can count these valid pairs in O(n log n).

title: My Calendar III
description: Design a class that books events represented by [start, end) time intervals, and returns the maximum number of overlapping events (the k-booking count) after each new booking is added — no bookings are ever rejected.
constraints:
0 <= start < end <= 10^9
At most 400 calls to book

examples.explanation: Each call returns the maximum overlap count across all bookings made so far
Each new booking increases the max overlap by exactly 1 since they all pairwise overlap

hints: A brute-force approach re-scans overlap counts for every existing event on each new booking — this can be slow for many bookings.
Think of this as a range-update problem: booking [start, end) increments a coverage count over that whole range, and you need the running maximum coverage.

A segment tree supporting range increment updates and range maximum queries (with lazy propagation) handles this efficiently, or, given the small call limit here, even a coordinate-compressed difference-array approach with a sweep to recompute the max after each booking is a workable simpler alternative.

title: LRU Cache
description: Design a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache that supports get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) average time, evicting the least recently used item when capacity is exceeded.
constraints:
1 <= capacity <= 3000
0 <= key, value <= 10^4
At most 2*10^5 calls to get and put

examples.input: LRUCache(2), put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4)
examples.explanation: Adding a 3rd item evicts key 2 (least recently used after get(1) refreshed key 1); adding a 4th evicts key 1

examples.input: LRUCache(1), put(2,1), get(2), put(3,2), get(2), get(3)
examples.explanation: With capacity 1, adding key 3 evicts key 2 immediately

hints: A hash map alone gives O(1) lookup but doesn't track recency order; a plain linked list tracks order but has O(n) lookup — you need both together.
Combine a hash map (key -> node) with a doubly linked list, where the list order represents recency (most recently used at one end, least at the other).

On get(), move the accessed node to the most-recently-used end. On put(), if at capacity, remove the node at the least-recently-used end before inserting the new one — both operations are O(1) since the doubly linked list allows removal/insertion at any known node without traversal.

title: All O(1) Data Structure
description: Design a data structure that stores strings with associated counts, supporting insert (increment count, insert if new), delete (decrement count, remove if it hits 0), getMaxKey (any key with the highest count), and getMinKey (any key with the lowest count), all in O(1) time.
constraints:
1 <= key.length <= 10
key consists of lowercase English letters
At most 5*10^4 calls total to insert, delete, getMaxKey, and getMinKey

examples.input: inc("hello"), inc("hello"), getMaxKey(), getMinKey(), inc("leet"), getMaxKey(), getMinKey()
examples.explanation: After two increments, 'hello' has count 2 and is both max and min until 'leet' is added with count 1
After incrementing then decrementing 'a' to 0, it's removed, leaving no keys, so both return an empty string

hints: A hash map from key to count gives O(1) count lookup, but finding max/min counts naively requires scanning all keys — you need a structure that tracks counts in order too.
Maintain a doubly linked list of 'buckets', each representing a distinct count value and holding the set of keys currently at that count, kept sorted by count from one end to the other.

When a key's count changes, move it from its current bucket to the adjacent bucket (creating a new bucket if needed, removing the old one if it becomes empty) — this keeps insert, delete, getMaxKey, and getMinKey all O(1).

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
description: Design a data structure that supports insert(val), remove(val), and getRandom() — returning a uniformly random element from the current elements — all in average O(1) time.
constraints:
-2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1
At most 2*10^5 calls total to insert, remove, and getRandom
At least one element exists whenever getRandom is called

examples.input: insert(1), remove(2), insert(2), getRandom(), remove(1), insert(2)
examples.output: true, false, true, 1 or 2, true, false
examples.explanation: remove(2) fails since 2 wasn't present yet; insert(2) after that succeeds; getRandom returns whichever element remains uniformly at random; the final insert(2) fails since 2 is already present
After removing 0, only 1 remains, so getRandom always returns 1

hints: A hash set alone supports O(1) insert/remove/contains, but doesn't support O(1) uniformly random access since sets aren't indexable.
Combine an array (for O(1) indexed random access) with a hash map from value to its index in the array.

To remove in O(1), swap the element to remove with the last element in the array, update the swapped element's index in the map, then pop the last element — this avoids the O(n) shifting a normal array removal would require.

title: LFU Cache
description: Design a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache that supports get(key) and put(key, value) in O(1) average time, evicting the least frequently used item when capacity is exceeded (breaking ties by least recently used among equally frequent items).
constraints:
0 <= capacity <= 10^4
0 <= key, value <= 10^5
At most 2*10^5 calls to get and put

examples.input: LFUCache(2), put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3), get(2), get(3), put(4,4), get(1), get(3), get(4)
examples.explanation: Key 2 has the lowest frequency (never accessed after insertion) so it's evicted when key 3 is added; later key 1 gets evicted since it's tied in frequency with key 3 but was used less recently
A capacity of 0 means nothing can ever be stored

hints: This extends LRU Cache by adding a second dimension: frequency of use, not just recency.

Maintain a hash map from key to (value, frequency), and a second structure mapping each frequency count to an ordered list (or doubly linked list) of keys with that frequency, ordered by recency within that frequency.

Track the current minimum frequency across all keys; on eviction, remove the least-recently-used key from the minimum-frequency bucket. On every get or put (update), increment that key's frequency and move it to the next frequency bucket, updating the minimum frequency tracker as needed.

title: Top K Frequent Words
description: Given an array of strings and an integer k, return the k most frequent strings, sorted by frequency (highest first); for equal frequency, sort lexicographically (ascending).
constraints:
1 <= words.length <= 500
1 <= words[i].length <= 10
1 <= k <= number of distinct words

examples.explanation: "i" and "love" both appear twice, which is the highest frequency, and "i" comes before "love" alphabetically
Sorted by descending frequency, with ties broken alphabetically

hints: First count word frequencies with a hash map — that part is standard.
A heap (priority queue) sorted by frequency descending, then lexicographically ascending as a tiebreaker, lets you extract the top k efficiently without a full sort.

Alternatively, since word counts are naturally bounded, sorting all distinct words with a custom comparator (frequency descending, then alphabetical) and taking the first k also works within these constraints.

title: Design Most Recently Used Queue
description: Design a queue-like structure of n elements (initially 1 to n) that supports fetching the kth element from the front and moving it to the very end (most recently used position), returning the fetched value.
constraints:
1 <= n <= 3000
1 <= k <= n
At most 1000 calls to fetch

examples.explanation: Each fetch retrieves the kth element from the current front and moves it to the end, changing subsequent positions
After the first fetch moves 3 to the end, the sequence becomes [1,2,4,5,3]; the 3rd element is now 4

hints: A plain array requires O(n) to remove an element from the middle and append it — acceptable within these constraints, but think about why a more advanced structure would be needed at larger scale.
For these constraints, maintaining a simple list and doing the remove-and-append operation directly (O(n) per fetch) is a reasonable and correct approach.

Simulate directly: find the kth element (1-indexed) from the front, remove it, and push it to the back, returning its value — this reinforces the underlying 'move to most-recently-used position' pattern shared with LFU/LRU design.

title: Logger Rate Limiter
description: Design a logger system that receives a stream of messages along with their timestamps. A message should be printed only if it wasn't already printed in the last 10 seconds (any duplicate message within that window is suppressed).
constraints:
0 <= timestamp <= 10^9
Every timestamp is passed in non-decreasing order
At most 10^4 calls to shouldPrintMessage

examples.input: shouldPrintMessage(1,"foo"), shouldPrintMessage(2,"bar"), shouldPrintMessage(3,"foo"), shouldPrintMessage(8,"bar"), shouldPrintMessage(10,"foo"), shouldPrintMessage(11,"foo")
examples.output: true, true, false, false, false, true
examples.explanation: 'foo' at timestamp 3 is suppressed (within 10s of timestamp 1); at timestamp 11, 10 seconds have passed since timestamp 1, so it's allowed again
20 seconds apart is beyond the 10-second window, so both print

hints: A hash map from message to its last-printed timestamp lets you check and update in O(1) per call.
On each call, look up the message's last printed timestamp; if it doesn't exist, or the current timestamp is at least 10 seconds after it, allow it and update the stored timestamp.
Since timestamps arrive in non-decreasing order, you don't need to worry about out-of-order edge cases, simplifying the comparison logic to a straightforward difference check.

title: Design Hit Counter
description: Design a hit counter that counts the number of hits received in the past 5 minutes (300 seconds), supporting hit(timestamp) to record a hit and getHits(timestamp) to query the count, with timestamps arriving in non-decreasing order.
constraints:
1 <= timestamp <= 2*10^9
All calls arrive in chronological (non-decreasing timestamp) order
At most 300 calls to hit and getHits combined

examples.input: hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), getHits(4), hit(300), getHits(300), getHits(301)
examples.explanation: getHits(300) counts hits within [1,300], which includes all 4 hits; getHits(301) counts hits within [2,301], excluding the hit at timestamp 1
A single hit counted immediately

hints: A naive approach storing every individual hit timestamp in a list, then filtering on each query, is simple but can be memory- and time-heavy for many hits.
A more efficient design uses a fixed-size circular buffer of 300 slots, one per possible second within the window, storing (timestamp, count) pairs.

On hit(), if the slot for (timestamp % 300) already stores a different (stale) timestamp, reset that slot's count to 1 with the new timestamp; otherwise increment it. On getHits(), sum the counts of all slots whose stored timestamp falls within the last 300 seconds.

title: Design a Token Bucket Rate Limiter
description: Design a rate limiter using the token bucket algorithm: a bucket holds up to a maximum number of tokens, refilling at a fixed rate over time; each request consumes one token if available (allowed) or is rejected if the bucket is empty.
constraints:
1 <= maxTokens <= 10^4
1 <= refillRatePerSecond <= 10^4
Requests arrive with non-decreasing timestamps

examples.input: TokenBucket(maxTokens=3, refillRate=1), allowRequest(t=0), allowRequest(t=0), allowRequest(t=0), allowRequest(t=0), allowRequest(t=1)
examples.explanation: The bucket starts full with 3 tokens; the 4th request at t=0 is rejected since the bucket is empty; by t=1, one token has refilled, allowing the 5th request
With only 1 max token, the second immediate request is rejected until a refill occurs at t=1

hints: Rather than actively refilling tokens on a timer, compute the number of tokens that should have accumulated lazily, at the moment each request arrives.
On each request, calculate elapsed time since the last check, add (elapsed * refillRate) tokens to the bucket (capped at maxTokens), then check if at least one token is available.

If a token is available, consume one and allow the request; otherwise reject it — update the 'last checked' timestamp on every request regardless of outcome, so refill calculations stay accurate going forward.

title: Search Suggestions System
description: Given an array of product names and a search word, return a list of up to 3 lexicographically smallest products that share a common prefix with the search word after each character the user types.
constraints:
1 <= products.length <= 1000
1 <= products[i].length <= 3000
1 <= searchWord.length <= 1000
All strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: After typing each prefix 'm','mo','mou','mous','mouse', the top 3 lexicographically smallest matches are returned
With only one product matching every prefix, it appears in every suggestion list

hints: Sorting all products lexicographically upfront makes 'top 3 smallest matching a prefix' much easier to find at each step.
Build a Trie of all products, where each Trie node stores (or can look up) the up-to-3 lexicographically smallest complete words passing through it.

As you type each character of searchWord, walk one more step into the Trie; if at any point the path breaks (no matching node), all remaining suggestion lists are simply empty for the rest of the word.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
description: Design a data structure that supports adding words and searching for a word, where the search word may contain '.' as a wildcard matching any single letter.
constraints:
1 <= word.length <= 25
word consists of lowercase English letters and possibly '.' in search queries
At most 10^4 calls total to addWord and search

examples.input: addWord("bad"), addWord("dad"), addWord("mad"), search("pad"), search("bad"), search(".ad"), search("b..")
examples.explanation: '.ad' matches any 3-letter word ending in 'ad'; 'b..' matches any 3-letter word starting with 'b'
A single '.' matches any single-character word

hints: A standard Trie handles exact-letter matching naturally, but the '.' wildcard requires trying every possible branch at that position.
addWord() works exactly like a normal Trie insert.

search() needs a recursive/backtracking traversal: for a normal letter, follow the matching child (if it exists); for '.', try ALL children at that position and return true if any of them lead to a successful match for the rest of the word.

title: Replace Words
description: Given a dictionary of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence that has a root from the dictionary as a prefix with that (shortest) root, leaving words without a matching root unchanged.
constraints:
1 <= dictionary.length <= 1000
1 <= dictionary[i].length <= 100
1 <= sentence.length <= 10^6
All strings consist of lowercase English letters

examples.input: dictionary = ["cat","bat","rat"], sentence = "the cattle was rattled by the battery"
examples.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"
examples.explanation: Each word in the sentence that starts with a dictionary root gets replaced by that root
Every word gets replaced by its shortest matching single-letter root

hints: Build a Trie from all the dictionary roots, marking the end of each root word.

For each word in the sentence, walk through the Trie character by character; the moment you hit a node marked as 'end of root', you've found the shortest matching root — stop there and use it as the replacement.
If you walk through the entire word without ever hitting a marked 'end of root' node, the word has no matching root and should be left unchanged.

testCases.input: ["cat","bat","rat"]|"the cattle was rattled by the battery"
testCases.output: "the cat was rat by the bat"

title: Min Stack
description: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, all in O(1) time.
constraints:
-2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1
Methods pop, top, and getMin are called only on non-empty stacks
At most 3*10^4 calls total

examples.input: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin(), pop(), top(), getMin()
examples.explanation: After popping -3, the stack is [-2,0], whose minimum is -2
The minimum stays 1 even after popping 2, since 1 remains on the stack

hints: A single stack alone can't tell you the current minimum in O(1) without scanning — you need to track minimums alongside the main data.
Maintain a second 'min stack' that tracks the minimum value at each point in time, pushing a new minimum (or a repeat of the current minimum) every time you push to the main stack.
When popping from the main stack, pop from the min stack too — this keeps both stacks perfectly synchronized, so the top of the min stack is always the current overall minimum in O(1).

title: Max Stack
description: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, retrieving the maximum element, and popMax (removing and returning the maximum element, keeping the relative order of the remaining elements intact), all efficiently.
constraints:
-10^7 <= val <= 10^7
At most 10^4 calls total to all methods
Methods pop, top, peekMax, and popMax are called only on non-empty stacks

examples.input: push(5), push(1), push(5), top(), popMax(), top(), peekMax(), pop(), top()
examples.explanation: popMax() removes the last (topmost) occurrence of the maximum value 5, preserving stack order for the rest
After removing the max (3), the new top is 2

hints: Unlike Min Stack, popMax() requires removing an element from the MIDDLE of the stack (conceptually) while preserving order — a plain array-backed stack alone struggles with O(1) removal from an arbitrary position.

A common approach: use a doubly linked list for the main stack (allowing O(1) removal given a node reference) paired with a sorted structure (like a TreeMap/balanced BST keyed by value, mapping to a stack of node references with that value) to quickly find and remove the current maximum.

When popMax() is called, look up the maximum value's most recent node reference, unlink it directly from the doubly linked list (in O(1) given the reference), and remove that reference from the sorted structure — keeping the rest of the stack's relative order untouched.

title: Design a Stack With Increment Operation
description: Design a stack with a fixed maximum capacity that supports push, pop, and an increment operation that adds a given value to the bottom k elements of the stack (or all elements if fewer than k exist), all efficiently.
constraints:
1 <= maxSize <= 1000
1 <= x <= 1000
0 <= k <= 1000
0 <= val <= 100
At most 1000 calls total to push, pop, and increment

examples.input: CustomStack(3), push(1), push(2), pop(), push(2), push(3), push(4), increment(5,100), increment(2,100), pop(), pop(), pop(), pop()
examples.explanation: increment(5,100) adds 100 to the bottom 5 (or fewer) elements; a 4th push is rejected since maxSize is 3, and a pop beyond empty returns -1
The 3rd push is rejected due to capacity 2, so pop returns the top of [1,2], which is 2

hints: Directly updating the bottom k elements on every increment() call is straightforward but can be O(k) per call — often acceptable, but think about how you'd optimize it further.
A simple array-backed stack, respecting the maxSize limit on push, handles push/pop naturally; increment() can loop through the bottom min(k, current size) elements and add the value directly.

For an optimized O(1) increment, instead maintain a separate 'lazy increment' array where incNeeded[i] represents a pending amount to add to the element at stack position i (and everything below it) — applying and propagating this lazily only when elements are actually popped.
